props.title: All the Colors of the Dark
props.initialSlug: Woman's nightmares lead to a sinister occult cult

sections.content: All the Colors of the Dark (1972) stands as a pivotal entry in the giallo movement, featuring Edwige Fenech in one of her most haunting performances. Director Sergio Martino crafts a hallucinatory nightmare that pushes beyond standard giallo tropes into psychological horror territory. The film shares DNA with Rosemary's Baby (1968) and anticipates the paranoid occult thrillers of the 1970s like The Wicker Man (1973), but adds distinctly Italian flourishes - saturated colors, elaborate murder sequences, and a hypnotic Bruno Nicolai score that rivals Ennio Morricone's best work.

sections.content: The film's exploration of cults and psychological manipulation connects directly to contemporaneous works like The Other (1972) and Don't Look Now (1973). Martino's direction creates a destabilizing effect through canted angles, extreme close-ups, and a color palette that shifts between naturalistic tones and psychedelic excess. The film's treatment of trauma and recovery through Jane's character (Fenech) predates similar themes in Suspiria (1977) and Possession (1981). SUBHEAD: Evolution of Italian Horror Cinema

Martino's work bridges classic giallo and the more experimental horror films of the mid-1970s. While Deep Red (1975) and Tenebrae (1982) would later perfect the giallo formula, All the Colors of the Dark took bold risks by incorporating supernatural elements and explicit occult imagery. This hybrid approach influenced later films like Inferno (1980) and The Beyond (1981), which similarly mixed giallo elements with supernatural horror.
